title: Hunting and fixing flaky tests
summary: Reproduce a flake on purpose (repeat runs, random order, one test alone, a loaded machine), then fix the cause: await the real signal instead of sleeping, isolate state, control the environment.

steps.title: Make it fail on demand
body: You cannot fix what you cannot reproduce. Ways to make a flaky test fail on your machine:

- **Repeat it**: run just that test 200 times. Bash: `for i in $(seq 200); do dotnet test --project Shop.Tests --filter-method "*Sends_all*" || break; done`. PowerShell: `1..200 | % { dotnet test ...; if ($LASTEXITCODE) { break } }`.
- **Run it alone, then with its neighbours**: passes alone and fails with the class means shared state. Bisect the other tests until you find the polluter.
- **Change the order**: xUnit v3 randomises with a seed it prints in the output; pass the same seed back (`--seed 1234`) to replay a failing run exactly.
- **Stress the machine**: run with `--parallel all` (or start a CPU-heavy job beside it): timing bugs show up when the scheduler is slow.

- **Hangs**: the MTP hang-dump extension (`--hangdump --hangdump-timeout 5m`) writes a memory dump and the stacks of a test that never finishes; VSTest's equivalent is `--blame-hang-timeout 5m`. `--crashdump` (or `--blame-crash`) catches a test host that dies.
Then fix the cause, never the symptom. For async code the rule is simple: **wait for the signal, not for the clock**.
await Task.Delay(50);              // flaky: hopes the worker is done
await outbox.DrainAsync();         // deterministic: completes when the worker has finished
If the code under test offers no completion signal, that is a design problem worth fixing: production needs it too, for a graceful shutdown.

steps.prompt: A test fails about once a week on CI. Order the investigation.
lines: Read the failure message and stack trace of the red runs
Run the test alone in a loop to see whether it fails on its own
Run it with its class and the whole suite to look for shared state
Form a hypothesis (time, order, async, environment) and make it fail on demand
Fix the cause and keep a repeat run green before merging
steps.explain: Evidence first, then isolation, then a reproduction you control. A fix you cannot make fail beforehand is a guess.

steps.prompt: `ExportTests.Writes_csv` passes 200 times in a row alone, and fails one time in ten when the whole suite runs. What should you look for first?
options: Another test that uses the same file path or shared state (bisect the suite to find it)
A bug in the CSV writer's rounding
steps.explain: Passing alone and failing in company is the signature of shared state. Give each test its own folder (`Directory.CreateTempSubdirectory`) and the interaction disappears.

steps.title: Wait for the signal, not the clock
prompt: The outbox sends messages from a background worker and retries a failed send once. It is compiled beside your tests:
if (await TrySend(send, message) || await TrySend(send, message)) lock (sent) sent.Add(message);
static async Task<bool> TrySend(Func<string, Task> send, string message)
public async Task DrainAsync() { channel.Writer.Complete(); await worker; }   // finishes when every message is handled
public IReadOnlyList<string> Sent { get { lock (sent) return [.. sent]; } }
public IReadOnlyList<string> Failed { get { lock (failed) return [.. failed]; } }

The starter waits with `Task.Delay` and is flaky. Write `public class OutboxTests` with at least **4** tests that **await `DrainAsync()`** before asserting: everything is sent in order; a send that fails once is retried and succeeds; a send that fails twice ends in `Failed`; nothing is sent twice. Four planted bugs. No sleeps or delays.
solution: var outbox = new Outbox(_ => ++attempts == 1 ? throw new HttpRequestException("503") : Task.CompletedTask);
var outbox = new Outbox(_ => throw new HttpRequestException("503"));
var outbox = new Outbox(m => { lock (calls) calls.Add(m); return Task.CompletedTask; });

target: if (await TrySend(send, message) || await TrySend(send, message)) lock (sent) sent.Add(message);
static async Task<bool> TrySend(Func<string, Task> send, string message)
public async Task DrainAsync() { channel.Writer.Complete(); await worker; }
public IReadOnlyList<string> Sent { get { lock (sent) return [.. sent]; } }
public IReadOnlyList<string> Failed { get { lock (failed) return [.. failed]; } }

mutants.name: a failed send counts as sent

forbid.message: No sleeps or delays: await DrainAsync

hints: Enqueue, then `await outbox.DrainAsync();`, then assert on `Sent` and `Failed`. The order of statements is the whole fix.
A send that fails once: `var attempts = 0; new Outbox(_ => ++attempts == 1 ? throw new HttpRequestException("503") : Task.CompletedTask)`.
A send that always fails: `new Outbox(_ => throw new HttpRequestException("503"))`, and the message must end up in `Failed`.
steps.explain: `DrainAsync` returns only when the worker has handled every message, so the assertions run at a moment you control: the tests pass on a fast laptop and a starved CI agent alike.
